title: Praying for healing
hookLine: Pentecostals pray boldly for healing, trusting God with the outcome

cards: That question sits in the letter of James, and the instructions that follow are practical: call the elders of the church, and let them pray over the sick person, anointing with oil in the name of the Lord.
In a Pentecostal service, it can be very direct. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who is ill to come forward. Elders gather.

Someone brings a small bottle of oil. Hands rest on shoulders, and the prayers are bold: out loud, by name, asking God to heal this body, this week. Then everyone goes home and lives with whatever happens next.

teach.b: James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up." Pentecostal churches take that at its word: if the letter says ask, ask out loud.

teach.h: WITH HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED.
teach.b: Today's line echoes Isaiah's song of a servant who suffers for others: "he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."
Stripes here are the welts a beating leaves on skin. The New Testament reads this song through Jesus, beaten and crucified, in two directions.
Matthew, after Jesus heals a crowd one evening, quotes the verse just before: "Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses."
Peter's first letter quotes the stripes line itself, right after saying Christ bore our sins, "that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness." So Christians read it more than one way.

teach.h: THE BODY, THE SOUL, OR BOTH?
teach.b: Some Pentecostals hold that healing for the body is part of what Christ won on the cross, and pray with that confidence.

Other Christians read the stripes first as healing from sin, and see bodily healing as a gift God gives as he wills. Catholic and Orthodox Christians draw on James for a sacrament of anointing the sick.
And then there's Paul, with what he called a thorn in the flesh: "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me."
The answer he records: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Bold asking, and open hands about the answer. Pentecostal prayer for healing tries to hold both.

how: In Pentecostal churches, the sick are often invited forward during or after a service, and elders or the congregation lay hands on them, sometimes anoint them with oil, and pray aloud for healing; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also practice a sacrament of anointing the sick.

o: asking God boldly to heal, and trusting God with what comes
a church collection to cover a sick member's bills
a medical treatment a church blesses before it is used

games.q: asking for healing — tap the pairs.

s: James tells the sick to call the elders of the church
and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.
in Isaiah, stripes are a pattern of lines
they're the welts a beating leaves: the servant is wounded and bruised.
Paul says his thorn was taken away when he prayed
the answer he records is "my grace is sufficient for thee."

games.q: you're Paul. you have a thorn in the flesh, and you've asked the Lord three times to take it away. what answer does your letter record?
o: my grace is sufficient for thee.
games.why: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Paul asked boldly, and wrote down an answer he hadn't asked for.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is ill right now, say their name quietly, and see where they are this minute: a hospital bed, a couch, a waiting room.
If you pray, ask God plainly for their healing, by name, the way James's elders did, and leave the outcome in God's hands. If you don't, hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Praying for healing. Asking God boldly to heal, as James describes, while trusting God with what comes.

orig.note: Hebrew, in Isaiah 53:5: a welt or bruise, the mark a blow leaves. The King James renders it stripes.

carryVoice: Your line: by his stripes. The welts of a beating, read by Christians as healing. Go gently.
